title: Positive square roots and their uniqueness
subtitle: G2 lecture 034000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded companion deck developed from the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix. Adds explicit mathematical formulas, worked examples, and topic-specific diagrams while remaining standalone.

slides.title: Why square roots matter
slides.lead: For a positive operator A, there is a canonical positive operator whose square is A.
body: This is the operator version of the elementary fact that a nonnegative real number has a unique nonnegative square root. The spectral theorem lets us carry that scalar construction over to positive matrices.
The result is central because it later defines the modulus |T|=(T* T)^{1/2} and supports polar decomposition.
slides.takeaway: Positive square roots are a canonical consequence of positivity and spectral calculus.

slides.title: Entrywise square roots are the wrong idea
slides.lead: Operator square roots are not obtained by taking square roots of the entries one by one.
body: A positive matrix may have negative off-diagonal entries, so entrywise square roots may not even be real. More importantly, the property we need is B² = A, which is a matrix equation, not an entrywise one.
The correct construction acts on eigenvalues after diagonalizing A, not on the raw matrix entries.
slides.takeaway: The square root belongs to the spectrum of A, not to its entries.

slides.title: Constructing the square root
slides.lead: If A = Σ λ P_λ with λ ≥ 0, define the root by applying t ↦ √t to the spectrum.
body: Because every spectral value is nonnegative, each scalar square root is well defined. Squaring the operator multiplies each eigenspace by (√λ)² = λ, so the result is exactly A.
The same spectral projections appear; only the scalar labels on those eigenspaces change.
slides.takeaway: Positive square roots are a direct application of finite functional calculus.

slides.title: A hand-checkable example
slides.lead: Take A = diag(9,4). Its positive square root should be immediate.
body: Squaring diag(3,2) returns diag(9,4), and the operator is positive because its spectrum is {3,2}. This diagonal example captures the general mechanism: the root keeps the eigenspaces and takes square roots of the spectral values.
If the matrix is merely diagonalizable by an orthonormal basis, the same story holds after conjugating into diagonal form and back.
slides.takeaway: The root keeps eigendirections and transforms λ into √λ.

slides.title: Why the positive square root is unique
slides.lead: Among positive operators, there is only one square root of A.
body: Suppose B and C are positive and B² = C² = A. Positivity implies that B and C are self-adjoint with nonnegative spectrum, so each can be written through the spectral calculus for A.

On every λ-eigenspace of A, the possible scalar roots are ±√λ, but positivity rules out the negative choice. Therefore both operators act by the same scalar √λ on every spectral subspace, forcing B = C.
slides.takeaway: Positivity removes the sign ambiguity that scalar square roots normally have.

slides.title: Zero eigenspaces cause no problem
slides.lead: If A kills some directions, the square root kills exactly those same directions.
body: On the 0-eigenspace, the scalar square root is again 0, so the square root acts trivially there. Nothing singular happens; the kernel simply persists.
This fact becomes useful later when we form |T| = (T* T)^{1/2}. The kernel of |T| agrees with the kernel of T because both are determined by the zero spectral component.
slides.takeaway: The square root preserves the zero spectral subspace exactly.

slides.title: Two rules worth remembering
slides.lead: Once defined spectrally, the positive square root inherits useful compatibility rules.
body: The first identity is the defining property. The second says that unitary changes of coordinates commute with taking the positive square root. Both statements follow because spectral projections and spectral values transform compatibly under unitary conjugation.
These identities are often the quickest way to recognize a candidate square root in practice.
slides.takeaway: Square roots are canonical and coordinate-free, not artifacts of one basis.

slides.title: Why commuting operators behave well
slides.lead: An operator that commutes with A also commutes with A^{1/2}.
body: The reason is again spectral. Commuting with A means preserving each spectral subspace of A, hence commuting with every spectral projection P_λ. Therefore it also commutes with any operator built from those projections, including A^{1/2}.
This stability will let us move square roots through several later constructions without reopening the definition every time.
slides.takeaway: Functional-calculus operators inherit the spectral symmetries of A.

slides.title: Bridge to modulus and singular values
slides.lead: The main downstream application is to the positive operator T* T.
body: For any linear map T, the Gram operator T* T is positive, so it has a unique positive square root. That square root is the modulus |T|. Its eigenvalues are the singular values of T, and it measures the lengths of outputs produced by T.
So the present lecture is the exact algebraic preparation for singular-value decomposition and polar decomposition.
slides.takeaway: Positive square roots are not optional decoration; they create the modulus of an operator.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.lead: Recover the whole theorem from the spectral theorem.
body: If A is positive, all its eigenvalues are nonnegative. Keep the same spectral projections and replace each λ by √λ. The result is a positive operator whose square is A. No other positive operator can square to A, because positivity forces the positive scalar branch on each eigenspace.
That is the entire square-root theorem in one sentence.
slides.takeaway: Existence comes from spectral calculus; uniqueness comes from positivity.
